name: MCP65R46T-2402E_CHY
title: MCP65R41/6: 3 µA comparator with integrated 1.21 V or 2.4 V reference, push-pull or open-drain output, SOT-23-6
summary: A single low-power CMOS comparator that also brings out an on-chip reference of 1.21 V or 2.4 V (±1% typical) on its own pin. It runs from 1.8 V to 5.5 V on 2.5 µA typical, accepts inputs 0.3 V beyond both rails, has about 3.3 mV of built-in hysteresis and switches in about 4 µs with 100 mV overdrive. The MCP65R41 has a push-pull output; the MCP65R46 has an open-drain output that can be pulled up to as much as 10 V. MCP65R46T-2402E/CHY is the open-drain, 2.4 V reference part in SOT-23-6 on tape and reel.
key_figures: 2.5 µA typ, 4 µA max per comparator
4 µs typ, 8 µs max at 100 mV overdrive

notes: Order code fields: device (MCP65R41T push-pull, MCP65R46T open-drain, T for tape and reel), reference voltage (12 = 1.21 V, 24 = 2.4 V typical), reference tolerance (02 = 2%), temperature range (E), package (CHY).
The marking is two code letters followed by NN, a traceability code; an example part reads HV25.

circuits.title: Figure 1-1. Test circuit for the push-pull output comparators
circuits.description: Bench set-up behind the electrical tables for the MCP65R41. Two 200 kΩ resistors hold the non-inverting input at half the supply, the inverting input is driven by the test signal (at VSS when idle), and the output sees 200 kΩ to VDD and 200 kΩ to ground, which is 100 kΩ to VDD/2, plus 50 pF.

circuits.title: Figure 1-2. Test circuit for the open-drain comparators
circuits.description: Bench set-up behind the electrical tables for the MCP65R46: the same 200 kΩ divider on the non-inverting input, the test signal on the inverting input, a 2.74 kΩ pull-up from the output to VDD, and 100 kΩ with 50 pF from the output to ground.

circuits.title: Figure 4-3. Protecting the analog inputs
circuits.description: Each input reaches its pin through a series resistor (R1, R2). A diode from each pin to VDD (D1, D2) catches excursions above the supply, the chip's own ESD diodes catch those below ground, and the resistors cap the current through both. R3 is feedback from the output to the inverting input.

parts.note: Fitted only with the open-drain MCP65R46.

circuits.title: Figure 4-4. Non-inverting circuit with hysteresis for single supply
circuits.description: Hysteresis set by two resistors on a single supply. The VREF pin feeds the inverting input; the signal reaches the non-inverting input through R1, and RF runs from the output back to that input. Example 4-1 gives the two trip points.

parts.note: Fitted only with the open-drain MCP65R46.

circuits.title: Figure 4-6. Inverting circuit with hysteresis
circuits.description: The signal goes straight to the inverting input. R2 and R3 divide VREF down onto the non-inverting input, and RF from the output to the same node shifts the threshold with the output state. The trip points follow from the Thevenin form of R2 and R3 (Figure 4-8, Equation 4-1).

parts.note: Fitted only with the open-drain MCP65R46.

circuits.title: Figure 4-10. Precise inverting comparator
circuits.description: For higher DC precision an MCP6041 op amp with R1 and R2 amplifies the input signal before it reaches the comparator, whose inverting input sits at VREF. The open-drain MCP65R46 with its pull-up also shifts the output to the VPU level.
notes: U2's VREF pin, U1's non-inverting input and U2's inverting input share the VREF node.

circuits.title: Figure 4-11. Bistable multi-vibrator
circuits.description: A multi-vibrator on one comparator: R1 from VREF and R2 from the output meet at the non-inverting input, and R3 from the output with C1 to ground sets the inverting input. VREF must lie between ground and 2.4 V for the circuit to oscillate, and the duty cycle moves with VREF.

circuits.title: Figure 4-12. Over-temperature alert circuit
circuits.description: R4 over a thermistor, both fed from the 2.4 V VREF pin, makes a temperature-dependent voltage on the inverting input. R2 and R3 divide the same reference for the alarm threshold on the non-inverting input, and RF from the output sets the hysteresis. Because every level comes from VREF, the thresholds hold still as a battery supply runs down.

parts.note: Fitted only with the open-drain MCP65R46.

operation.text: Each part carries a factory-trimmed reference on the VREF pin, 1.21 V or 2.4 V depending on the order code, typically within ±1% and within ±2% at the limits. The pin is a low-power output intended to feed the comparator inputs, directly or through a resistor divider. It is specified for about 200 pF of load; more than 2000 pF can make it oscillate at power-up.

The inputs are CMOS with very low bias current. Three differential pairs work in parallel, covering low, middle and high common-mode voltages, so the input range runs 0.3 V past each supply rail while the offset stays low across it. Offset is tested at VSS - 0.3 V and at VDD + 0.3 V.

About 3.3 mV of hysteresis is built in. It is small against the offset budget but large enough that the comparator's own input noise cannot make the output chatter; Figure 4-1 shows a slow triangle input giving clean output edges.

ESD diodes clamp an input that falls more than a diode drop below VSS or rises well above VDD. Input current must stay within ±2 mA. When the common-mode voltage goes below ground, considerable current can leave the inputs, which may restrict the usable range for high-impedance sources. Figure 4-3 adds series resistors and diodes to VDD; the diodes may instead sit on the source side of the resistors, provided something else limits their current, and the resistors then only limit inrush.
Driving the inputs beyond either supply rail does not invert the output (Figure 2-24).
The MCP65R41 output swings rail to rail and drives CMOS or TTL logic directly. Its drive circuit keeps supply-to-supply shoot-through small during output transitions.

The MCP65R46 output only sinks current and needs an external pull-up. The pull-up may go to any voltage from 1.6 V to 10 V, independent of VDD, so the part can translate logic levels; several outputs can share one pull-up as a wired-OR. A short on the output must not be to more than VSS + 10 V.

VDD sits 1.8 V to 5.5 V above VSS, and the other pins normally stay between the two rails. In single-supply use VSS is ground. Place a 0.01 µF to 0.1 µF bypass capacitor within 2 mm of the VDD pin for clean edges; a bulk capacitor shared with analog parts within 100 mm is optional.

Resistors around the comparator set wider, chosen trip points (Figures 4-4 and 4-6). This stops chatter on slowly moving inputs, keeps systems such as thermostats from switching too often, and saves the extra supply current that chatter draws.
Logic-gate loads barely change the propagation delay. Larger capacitance slows the output edges, lengthens the delay, and raises supply current as toggle frequency rises (Figures 2-20, 2-38, 2-41).

With 1 pA typical bias current at 25 °C, board leakage matters: about 10^12 Ω between nearby traces in dry conditions passes 5 pA at 5 V. A guard ring held at the potential of the sensitive input cuts this. In the inverting circuit, tie the ring to VIN+ and run VIN- to its pad inside the ring without touching it; in the non-inverting circuit, run VIN+ to its pad and tie the ring to VIN-.

Where more DC accuracy is wanted, an op amp such as the MCP6041 (600 nA, 14 kHz) amplifies the signal ahead of the comparator; with the MCP65R46 the output is also shifted to the VPU level (Figure 4-10).
In Figure 4-11 the circuit oscillates only when VREF lies between ground and 2.4 V; changing VREF changes the output duty cycle.
The 2.4 V reference biases the thermistor divider, the alarm threshold and the hysteresis network together, so the switching temperature does not drift as a battery supply sags (Figure 4-12).
